intro: Every day you use money without thinking about it: a card tapped at a gas station, a paycheck deposited by direct transfer, a few bills folded in a wallet. Behind each of those moments is a system most people never see. Banks take in deposits and lend them out. Lenders price loans with interest rates that decide whether a car payment is $483 or $495 a month. And a central bank, the Federal Reserve, with one of its twelve regional banks on LaSalle Street in Chicago, steers the cost of borrowing for the whole country.

This unit follows money from a jar on a dresser to a vote in Washington. The first chapter asks what money is, why a piece of paper with no gold behind it still buys groceries, how a bank turns one person's savings into another person's loan, and how simple and compound interest, APR and credit scores shape what borrowing really costs. The second chapter opens the Federal Reserve: who runs it, what goals Congress gave it, the tools it actually uses today, how a rate decision travels to a car lot in Peoria, and why its power is both shielded from politics and answerable to Congress.

By the end you will be able to name the three jobs of money, trace a deposit through the banking system with the money multiplier, compute simple and compound interest, compare loans by APR, explain the Fed's dual mandate and its 2% inflation target, predict which way rates, spending and prices move when the Fed eases or tightens, and weigh the main arguments about the Fed's independence.
bigQuestion: What makes money trustworthy, and how much should one central bank be allowed to shape what everyone pays to borrow?

timeline.t: Congress charters the First Bank of the United States, backed by Alexander Hamilton
The charter of the Second Bank of the United States expires after President Andrew Jackson's veto
Congress creates a system of nationally chartered banks and a national currency during the Civil War
A panic spreads through New York trust companies, and J. P. Morgan organizes private bankers to stop it
President Woodrow Wilson signs the Federal Reserve Act, creating twelve Reserve Banks, one in Chicago
After thousands of bank failures, Congress creates the FDIC to insure deposits
The United States stops exchanging dollars for gold with foreign governments
Congress writes maximum employment and stable prices into the Federal Reserve Act
Paul Volcker becomes Fed Chair and pushes rates toward 20% to break high inflation
In the financial crisis the Fed cuts its target to near zero and begins large bond purchases
The Fed announces a 2% inflation target
In the pandemic the Fed cuts rates to near zero again and sets reserve requirements to zero

words.d: something widely accepted in payment for goods and services
money that has value because a government declares it legal tender and people accept it, not because of what it is made of
a system in which banks keep only a fraction of deposits on hand and lend the rest
the maximum growth in deposits for each dollar of new reserves; equal to 1 divided by the reserve ratio
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per bank
interest paid on both the principal and the interest already earned
annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of a loan, including interest and most required fees
the Fed's two main goals set by Congress: maximum employment and stable prices
the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves
the Fed's buying and selling of government securities, which adds or removes reserves

test.q: Prices in a store are all posted in dollars. Which job of money does this show?
test.why: Stating all prices in one common measure is the unit-of-account job.

test.q: Today's U.S. dollar is best described as
choices: fiat money accepted because of confidence and a managed supply
test.why: The dollar is fiat money: it has no metal behind it and holds value through acceptance and the Fed's management of its supply.

test.q: A bank has $40,000 in new deposits and keeps 10% in reserve. How much can it lend?
test.why: Reserves are 10% of $40,000, or $4,000; the remaining $36,000 can be lent.

test.q: With a 10% reserve ratio, a new $5,000 deposit can create at most how much in total deposits?
test.why: The multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; $5,000 × 10 = $50,000 at the ceiling.

test.q: Why did runs on insured bank deposits nearly stop after 1934?
choices: Depositors no longer gained anything by withdrawing first
test.why: Deposit insurance guaranteed the money whether or not a depositor rushed, removing the reason to run.

test.q: You borrow $800 at 5% simple interest for three years. What is the total interest?
$1,000 earns 10% compounded yearly. What is the balance after two years?
test.why: Year one: $1,100. Year two: $1,100 × 1.10 = $1,210. The second year earns interest on the first year's interest.

test.q: A loan charges 1.5% per month. About what is its APR?
How many votes are on the Federal Open Market Committee?
test.why: Seven governors, the New York Fed president and four rotating Reserve Bank presidents: 7 + 1 + 4 = 12.

test.q: Which pair of goals makes up the Fed's dual mandate?
choices: Low taxes and a balanced budget
A strong dollar and high exports
test.why: Congress directed the Fed to pursue maximum employment and stable prices, which it defines as 2% inflation.

test.q: The Fed pays 4% on reserves. A bank is offered 3.5% to lend reserves overnight to another bank. What will it most likely do?
choices: Lend, because any interest is better than none
Lend, because the law requires it
Keep the reserves at the Fed and earn 4%
test.why: The rate on reserves is a risk-free floor; no bank lends for less than it can earn by leaving money at the Fed.

test.q: A bond pays $30 a year. Its price rises from $1,000 to $1,200. What is its new yield?
test.why: $30 ÷ $1,200 = 0.025, or 2.5%. The price rose, so the yield fell from 3%.

test.q: Inflation is 6% and the economy is running hot with very low unemployment. Which policy fits, and what does it do?
choices: Tightening, which raises borrowing costs and cools spending
Quantitative easing, which lowers long-term rates
Cutting reserve requirements, which expands lending
test.why: Inflation above target in a hot economy calls for contractionary policy: higher rates slow borrowing, spending and price increases.

test.q: A savings account pays 2% while inflation is 5%. What is the real interest rate?
test.why: Real rate = nominal minus inflation: 2% minus 5% is about negative 3%, so the savings lose buying power.

test.q: Which feature most directly shields Fed governors from political pressure?
choices: They are elected every two years
The Treasury pays their salaries each year
They serve 14-year terms and can be removed only for cause
test.why: Long terms and removal only for cause mean a governor cannot be fired for an unpopular rate decision.

write.prompt: Inflation is 5% and unemployment is 4.5% and rising slowly. You are a voting member of the FOMC. Argue for raising the target by 25 basis points or holding it steady. Use the dual mandate, the real interest rate, how a change would reach a $25,000 car loan, and policy lags, and name who gains and who pays under your choice.
tips: Compute the real interest rate before and after your choice, and say whether policy is easy or tight.
Trace the chain: Fed rate, bank rates, loan payments, spending, hiring, prices.
Name the trade-off between the two goals and which one you weigh more right now.
Remember the lag: your decision will not show its full effect for a year or more.
Answer the strongest argument against your choice.
